text: 59-year-old male. The patient presents to the emergency department with a sudden-onset sensation that the room is spinning, leading to several episodes of nausea and vomiting. text: I notice the previous questions were repeated, so I will proceed with new inquiries. Do you have any difficulty with balance, walking, or coordination, and did you experience any headache, double vision, or slurred speech during the episode? I need to rule out central causes like a stroke.

speaker: Doctor
text: Given the sudden onset and brief duration of your vertigo without neurological deficits or hearing loss, I need to perform a physical examination to provoke the symptoms. I will now perform the Dix-Hallpike maneuver to check for positional vertigo. REQUEST TEST: Dix-Hallpike Maneuver

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Positive, inducing nystagmus and reproducing patient’s symptoms of vertigo when head is turned to the left and laid back.

speaker: Doctor
text: The positive Dix-Hallpike maneuver on the left side strongly suggests Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV). I will now perform the Epley maneuver to treat the displaced crystals. REQUEST TEST: Epley Maneuver

speaker: Doctor
text: The Epley maneuver yielded normal readings, which is unexpected for typical BPPV given the positive Dix-Hallpike. I need to rule out other causes of acute vestibular syndrome. text: Since the Epley maneuver did not resolve the symptoms despite a positive Dix-Hallpike, I need to assess for central causes or other vestibular disorders. speaker: Doctor
text: The normal Head Impulse Test makes a peripheral vestibular lesion like vestibular neuritis less likely, suggesting a central cause despite the absence of obvious neurological deficits.
